name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
description: A subset of 23 particularly challenging BIG-Bench tasks for which no prior language model result outperformed the average human-rater score. The tasks require multi-step reasoning and include categories such as traditional NLP, mathematics, commonsense reasoning, and question-answering.
citeAs: Mirac Suzgun, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, Jason Wei. Challenging BIG-Bench tasks and whether chain-of-thought can solve them. arXiv:2210.09261v1 [cs.CL] 17 Oct 2022.
rai:dataCollection: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) was curated from the BIG-Bench benchmark by applying specific filtering criteria to identify challenging tasks. The filtering process selected 23 tasks (27 subtasks) from the original 209 BIG-Bench tasks based on criteria including: tasks with fewer than three subtasks, tasks with at least 103 examples, tasks with human-rater baselines, tasks using multiple-choice or exact match evaluation metrics, and tasks where no prior model outperformed the average human-rater score.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data comes from BIG-Bench (Beyond the Imitation Game Benchmark), a collaborative benchmark with over 200 diverse text-based tasks. BIG-Bench tasks were crowd-sourced and evaluated using several language model families (GPT-3, Gopher, PaLM) and human raters.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For all but three tasks in BBH, a random subset of 250 evaluation examples was taken. For Causal Judgement, Penguins in a Table, and Snarks, all available test examples (187, 146, and 178 respectively) were considered in addition to three examples reserved for few-shot prompting. The total benchmark contains 6,511 evaluation examples.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Tasks were filtered using the following criteria: (1) filtered out tasks with more than three subtasks, (2) filtered out tasks with fewer than 103 examples, (3) filtered out tasks without human-rater baselines, (4) filtered out tasks that do not use multiple-choice or exact match as evaluation metric, (5) filtered out tasks where the best reported model beats average reported human-rater score, (6) filtered out extremely difficult tasks outside the scope of the work (requiring domain-specific knowledge or not practically solvable within twenty minutes).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Chain-of-thought (CoT) exemplars were manually composed by the authors. Three chain-of-thought exemplars were created for each task in BBH. The phrase 'let's think step by step' was prepended to all CoT annotations in the few-shot exemplars. Task descriptions and answer options were included in prompts.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The data, prompts, and Codex model outputs are publicly available at https://github.com/suzgunmirac/BIG-Bench-Hard
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note that surpassing average human-rater performance on challenging tasks should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning. The paper acknowledges that the Moral Permissibility task was excluded because the authors did not want to delegate agency to models about moral judgement scenarios.
rai:dataLimitations: The human-rater scores are not fully representative of human performance. The human-evaluation component took almost a year, during which formatting and content of some tasks changed multiple times. Human-raters were allocated a few hours per day to solve a sub-sampled evaluation set and could use external resources such as the Internet. In some cases, task descriptions were hard to follow and could have been better-formulated. The authors acknowledge that human-rater performance and results should be interpreted with care. Some tasks (13 out of 36 initially identified) were excluded as extremely difficult, requiring domain-specific knowledge or not practically solvable within twenty minutes.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating language model capabilities on challenging reasoning tasks using few-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting. The benchmark is designed to test multi-step reasoning abilities and to measure whether chain-of-thought prompting can enable emergent task performance on tasks with otherwise flat scaling curves. The evaluation protocol uses greedy decoding with exact match accuracy measurement.
